# **1 INTRODUCTION**

## **1.1 Background of the Study** {#1.1-background-of-the-study}

The modern IT infrastructure brought about by rapid digitalization has redefined the landscape of how organizations handle data. This transition particularly underscored a need to shift from traditional printed storage to a more efficient data management, storage, and retrieval processes. Recent reports indicate that 80% of organizations intend to replace paper-based workflows with digital systems through different digital transformation initiatives; this transition specifies a major departure from traditional manual filing (SNS Insider, 2025). This shift is primarily driven by the inefficiencies that are present in the still-adopted outdated manual techniques, as these procedures are plagued with issues, such as slow execution and haphazard arrangement, thereby causing laborious work routines (Khan & Khanam, 2023).

On a global scale, digital transformation has become a major direction followed in public administration and institutional operations. In 2024, the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs assessed e-government development across all of the 193 United Nations Member States in its report entitled “E-Government Survey 2024”. The result of the assessment specifically suggested that the global average E-Government Development Index increased by 4.59% from 2022 to 2024, whereas the previous assessment merely concluded a 1.90% increase, thereby confirming how expansion of digital government initiatives continue worldwide (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs \[UN DESA\], 2024). The same report additionally emphasized the continued growth in terms of digital government by particularly listing the increased use of digital technologies in data management, integration of artificial intelligence, and the use of emerging technologies for policymaking as among the key concepts collectively referred to in this matter as global megatrends. These developments reinforce the expectedly increasing development, reliance, and maintenance of digital systems in information management.  This global movement reflects a growing consensus that digitized document management is no longer optional. 

The Philippine national government has likewise recognized the urgency of digitizing the operations in managing institutional records, as well as the procedures that administer government processes. In a recent venture, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) facilitated the accomplishment of various initiatives, such as the eGovernment Master Plan — a plan which aims to integrate technology-driven processes across public offices to enhance the overall service delivery. Also, as pointed out by Rodriguez et al. (2024) in their development of a document management and monitoring system for the Department of the Interior and Local Government, Negros Occidental, Philippines, named eDALAYON, many of these similar initiatives have arisen in the higher education section. It is an initiative system designed in response to the issues and challenges brought by poor document management practices in a governmental office. These actions collectively represent a continued effort to help Philippine institutions depart from the manual, paper-based record systems into more efficient, digitally managed repositories.

Bicol University is among the leading state universities in the Bicol Region. Within the university, the Office of Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) performs a central role in supporting institutional quality assurance activities by managing various reports, evaluations, policies, memoranda, accreditation-related records, and other supporting documents. The researchers first engaged with the IQA through an unstructured interview, which allowed the researchers to identify and explore the current practices of the office on document handling in an open manner. Specifically, this initial interview allowed the researchers to capture the office’s practices for document storage, requests, retrieval, and supervisory controls. To verify and improve the findings based on this first interview, the researchers conducted a secondary validation interview involving the IQA Office Director, two IQA members, and the clerical staff. With these data-gathering, it was revealed that the IQA office currently relies on a combination of printed documents stored in folders and cabinets, documents kept in a Google Drive repository, and spreadsheet-based tracking for monitoring of submissions. Document requests are usually commonly handled through email or face-to-face, therefore there is no formal tracking mechanism, no approval trail, and no status visibility for either the requestor or the IQA staff.  This is a fragmented approach. An approach like this complicates the document retrieval, version control, and traceability (Taufiqurrahman et al., 2025). As a consequence, the staffs are left with no choice but to check each record by record despite the substantial workload, especially during the accreditation of multiple college and university programs. In addition, specific accreditation-related documents, including accreditation recommendations, results, and supporting records, may exist in either printed or scanned form and therefore require manual scanning, uploading, and encoding before their contents can be reflected in a monitoring system (Mindoro-Mesana et al., 2023). This process adds to the workload of IQA staff and may delay the updating of submission statuses and compliance records.  Further, the lack of monitoring and notification capabilities exposes the office and the corresponding programs to delayed or possibly, missed submissions, especially during accreditation periods, where the issues are amplified due to the requirement submission becoming more critical — a negative impact on accreditation standings becomes possible. In this light, the identified tools currently used by the IQA, such as Google Drive and spreadsheet-based tracking, were not designed for document lifecycle management.

## **1.2 Objectives of the Study** {#1.2-objectives-of-the-study}

The study aims to design and develop a Document Management and Monitoring System for Bicol University Office of Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) to facilitate easy tracking of accreditations and easy access of documents. Specifically, the study aims to achieve the following:

1. To design and develop a centralized digital repository that allows authorized users to upload, organize, categorize, manage, update, and retrieve documents through search and filtering features, and to submit and process document requests through a structured workflow that IQA staff can review, approve, or deny accordingly. . 

2. To implement a monitoring component that enables authorized users to configure, track and monitor the document submission statuses and requirements of different university programs and institutions for accreditation compliance, receive automated notifications and reminders for upcoming and missed submission deadlines, and generate reports on document submission statuses, accreditation compliance progress, and monitoring activity across university programs and institutions. 

3. To integrate an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) feature that extracts printed text from scanned or uploaded accreditation-related documents to assist users in encoding accreditation results, submission details, and compliance-related information into the system. 

4. To determine the compliance of the developed system to ISO 25010 in terms of Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Compatibility, Usability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, and Portability.

## **1.3 Significance of the Study** {#1.3-significance-of-the-study}

This study holds a significant importance because it aims to develop a Document Management, Retrieval, and Monitoring System that will serve and help the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office of Bicol University to facilitate easy tracking of accreditations and easy access of documents. Specifically, the findings of this study are advantageous to the following:

**Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office.** The proposed system will directly benefit the IQA Office as it will provide a centralized digital repository for managing important documents such as policies, memorandums, and issuances. The system enables authorized personnel to upload, organize, retrieve, and track documents and required materials, as well as request documents efficiently. Furthermore, providing a system that will streamline processes will enhance document management efficiency and productivity while it decreases the need for manual file operations. Automatic updates will also increase the timely submission of required documents and their associated deadlines and will decrease the communication gaps.

 **Colleges, and Departments.** The system will enhance document management efficiency across colleges and departments by enabling authorized personnel to upload, organize, retrieve and request their files with ease. Through this document request module, the colleges and their departments will be able to submit requests for specific documents they need from the IQA Office easily. And this would also ensure that document access is properly tracked and managed. Notifying the college before an accreditation deadline will allow the colleges to take the necessary actions to ensure that the program is aligned with suggestions or recommendation requirements in a timely manner. 

**Academic Programs.** The system will prevent missed notifications of due requirements for accreditation, which keeps the program operational. 

**Finance Department.** The reaccreditation of a program requires funding before the reaccreditation deadline. By ensuring program compliance of requirements, the Finance Department can allocate the necessary budget before a visit, thus supplying the monetary needs of the program for accreditation.

**Bicol University.** As the institution where the IQArchive will be used, Bicol University will benefit from a more efficient and organized way of managing accreditation-related documents across colleges, departments and offices. Through modernization of the IQA’s document workflows, the university will be well equipped in responding to accreditation related requirements in a timely manner and systematic manner, strengthening its status as a top state university in the Bicol Region. 

**Community.** The study will benefit the community through its development of an effective document management system which will improve university operations and service delivery. The system helps Bicol University establish transparent and accountable Internal Quality Assurance processes while it improves the management of academic and administrative documents. The university will improve its educational and service quality through this development, which will create advantages for both students and all other university stakeholders and the local community.

**Researchers.** This study will benefit the researchers as the development of IQArchive serves as a fulfilment of a requirement for the completion of their academic course. The knowledge and experience gained from the study will further equip the researchers with relevant skills and insights that can be carried forward into their future lives. 

**Future Researchers.** This study shall serve as a reference source for future researchers who plan to study digital document management systems and centralized document storage systems. The work will deliver valuable information together with research techniques and research results, which will assist them in building better systems and performing additional research and extending their current study work in the future. 

## **1.4 Scope and Delimitations**  {#1.4-scope-and-delimitations}

This study aims to design, develop, and evaluate a Document Management and Monitoring System for the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office of Bicol University in order to make a convenient storage, access and tracking of documents and to improve the current processes of the office.

The scope of the study includes the design, development and evaluation of IQArchive as a web-based system. In terms of its function, the system offers a centralised digital repository through which authorised users can upload, organise, categorise, manage, update and retrieve documents relevant to policy memoranda, IQA office issuances and other accreditation-related records. Also a document request module will be included where authorised users can request specific papers which IQA staff can review, approve or deny as appropriate.

The system also offers a monitoring module in addition to the centralised repository, which allows authorised users to track and monitor the document submission statuses and accreditation compliance needs of different university programmes and institutions, receive automated notifications and reminders for upcoming and missed submission deadlines, and generate reports on submission statuses, accreditation compliance progress, and monitoring activity across university programmes and institutions.

In addition, the system has an OCR-assisted upload function to extract printed text from scanned or uploaded accreditation-related documents to enable faster encoding of accreditation results, submission details, and compliance-related information into the monitoring module.

The main users of IQArchive are those involved in accreditation and quality assurance at Bicol University: the staff in the IQA office who manage documents, check for compliance, and respond to document requests; and the heads of colleges, departments and academic programmes who submit documents, track compliance requirements for their units, and receive deadline notices. University officials and executives also can access the system for supervision and report viewing. The respondents will be IQA office personnel and IT specialists. To assess the quality of the system based on ISO 25010 compliance with the following factors: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Compatibility, Usability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, and Portability.

The limits of the study set the bounds for the development and evaluation of the system. IQArchive is restricted to document management and monitoring in support of accreditation compliance and does not handle other institutional management activities like payroll, human resource management, financial management or student data management. The system is not designed to be a university-wide document storage system and is limited to the operational scope of the IQA office and its accreditation-related procedures. The study does not cover the administrative activity of other offices of the university, or the internal flows of documents inside the colleges or departments, except for their accreditation tasks to the IQA office.

The OCR tool has technological restrictions in that it only extracts printed text. It does not recognise handwritten text and does not automatically check, interpret or confirm the correctness of accreditation findings. The user should check and correct the extracted text before saving it in the system. Finally, the study does not include the full-scale deployment and the long-term maintenance of the system. The scope of the study is limited to the design, development and early evaluation phases of the system development lifecycle.

# **2 THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK** {#2-theoretical-framework}

 In this chapter, the Review of Related Literature and Study, Concept of the Study, and the Definition of Terms were included and discussed. 

## **2.1 Review of Related Literature** {#2.1-review-of-related-literature}

	The proposed research addresses the need for an improved document management, retrieval, and monitoring for the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) office of Bicol University.

### **2.1.1 Web-Based Solutions** {#2.1.1-web-based-solutions}

With more organizations moving online, the need for purposeful systems with collaboration and sharing mechanisms have increased to manage institutional work across multiple interrelated offices. For instance, at universities, multiple departments are involved in the completion of tasks for quality assurance of documents. Web-based platforms help universities detach from cumbersome manual processes and move towards more efficient workflows.

The use of digital document systems is reported to help institutions achieve a smooth workflow due to the organized and systematic manner by which these systems allow users to approach document management. Using centralized storage, particularly, helps organizations easily upload, access, and protect their institutional records (Hermosa, 2023). These centralized storage further reinforce the improvement of intra-department connection, which is essential in the context of accreditation, as universities must ensure completeness and availability of necessary supporting documents to be submitted by individual institutions during accreditation periods (Galande, 2025). Further, a consolidated database makes it easier to keep track of submission, through which users can therefore be notified in case of missed deadlines to ensure they always meet the system's compliance requirements (Lemosnero et al., 2026). With the access to information improved by web-based systems, inter-office coordination and control of institutional work have become more possible.

### **2.1.2 Document Management System**  {#2.1.2-document-management-system}

Web-based systems make it easier for office staff to collaborate. With an increasing amount of records being created and shared digitally‚ the need for organization and management becomes paramount‚ especially at universities where many departments are creating and sharing such records․ A system is needed that will keep such records organized‚ protected and easily retrievable․ Document management systems serve these needs․

Document management systems may support all the features of records management throughout the entire lifecycle of the records‚ for example‚ creation‚ storage and retrieval‚ security tasks such as access management and audit (Han et al․‚ 2021)․ DMS can help reduce risks from manual filing of documents‚ such as loss or duplication‚ and improve workflow efficiency․ In practice‚ organizations that have adopted DMS are experiencing improved productivity and lower operating costs from the automation of ordinary processes (Alade‚ 2023)․

Document management systems also include later developments with more structured means of organization‚ allowing users to search for documents in a more subtle and precise way (Dres & Rabut‚ 2025)․ In the Philippines‚ document management systems have been shown to assist with administrative work and minimize mismanagement of documents in institutional settings (Nagrama et al․‚ 2024; Bobby Rodriguez III et al․‚ 2024)․ 

These studies show that while web-based platforms make it easier to access things, Document Management Systems make sure that information is organized and maintained in a way. However, when it is easy to store and get documents, institutions still have trouble keeping track of where the documents are and making sure they are submitted on time. Document management systems are important for this. This problem shows that institutions need systems to monitor and track documents. 

### **2.1.3 Document Monitoring and Tracking System** {#2.1.3-document-monitoring-and-tracking-system}

While document management systems help store and retrieve documents‚ there must be some method of tracking progress through the approval process and ensuring that documents are submitted on time․ This is particularly the case for colleges and universities which have to pay attention to accreditation deadlines for their departments․

Hermosa et al․ (2023) believed that incorporating tracking elements into document systems will help users track documents' movement‚ determine if they are on time and hold them accountable․ Lemosnero et al․ (2026) focused on quality control and proposed a tracking system that helps organizations ensure the quality of documents by monitoring compliance with mandatory standards and submission deadlines․ Merida et al․ (2026) found that features such as real-time tracking and automatic notifications that inform users of overdue or missing requirements and ensure the proper functioning of workflows are advantages of these technologies․ This eases the management of accreditation documents by allowing institutions to manage and process large amounts of documentation more efficiently‚ by improving visibility of their submission status (Mindoro-Mesana et al․‚ 2023)․

When documents are forwarded between departments or required by institutional bodies (such as accreditation)‚ tracking is necessary and can be achieved with systems that are easy to find and use․ Therefore‚ document management systems or similar systems for tracking documents should contain the tracking capabilities as well․

### **2.1.4 Optical Character Recognition** {#2.1.4-optical-character-recognition}

While web-based solutions, document management systems, and monitoring systems improve the storage, retrieval, and tracking of institutional documents, their effectiveness still depends on how quickly and accurately document information can be entered into the system. In accreditation monitoring, some results, recommendations, compliance forms, and supporting records may still come from printed or scanned documents. Uploading and encoding these materials is necessary before their details can be reflected in the monitoring records. If this is performed manually, it slows down the organizational workflow. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) can be used to assist users by extracting text from uploaded documents and will then lessen the time spent on encoding of accreditation results into the monitoring system.

The existing systems for accreditation-related documents have shown the need for organized document handling, but OCR is not always integrated. The Accreditation Document Management System of Apayao State College was developed by Galande (2025)․ While the authors sought to solve the problems of delayed access‚ unavailability‚ and the difficulties of storing‚ retrieving‚ submitting‚ sharing access to‚ and securing accreditation documents‚ the objectives and features do not directly address the OCR-assisted process of extracting information from scanned accreditation results․ However‚ this does indicate that while accreditation document systems support tracking and organizing documents‚ OCR was not commonly used to enable encoding of accreditation information․

Zain et al․ (2025) showed that OCR can also ease working with archives․ They designed an application for the Borobudur Subdistrict which uses Tesseract OCR to convert image documents into digital text․ This is followed by TextRank (Gao et al․‚ 2004\) and regular expressions to summarize its contents and find patterns․ The application increased the number of letters processed from 20 to 80 per day․ Pham et al․ (2022) used image deskewing‚ table recognition‚ and document layout analysis to improve the performance of an optical character recognition (OCR) system for scanned document management systems using the Tesseract OCR system․ They found a 23% increase in OCR accuracy when applying preprocessing to complex documents․ Singh & Middleton (2025) focused on complex tabular document types and proposed a tabular context-aware OCR for extraction of text information from complex tabular documents․ Their method‚ called TSC‚ combines Table Structure Recognition‚ TrOCR-ctx and ByT5 correction․ 

These studies show that OCR is useful in reducing manual encoding and converting scanned or printed documents into usable digital text. However, they also show that OCR is more commonly applied in archiving, scanned document management, or structured document extraction, rather than directly in accreditation monitoring systems. Accreditation document systems tend to focus on storage, retrieval, access control, submission, and monitoring, with little emphasis on OCR-assisted encoding. OCR can address a specific gap by helping users upload scanned accreditation results, recommendations, and supporting records more efficiently into the monitoring system. However, OCR accuracy may still be affected by blurred scans, skewed documents, low image quality, and complex layouts, so extracted text should still be reviewed and corrected by authorized users before being saved in the system.

### **2.1.5 Internal Quality Assurance in Higher Education** {#2.1.5-internal-quality-assurance-in-higher-education}

Accurate, organized, and accessible records are the guiding principles that allows internal quality assurance to accomplish its objectives of effective monitoring and validation. These records also serve as building blocks, upon which reports are formulated to guide the preparation for important operations, such as accreditation. In universities, this is crucial because quality assurance offices process documents from all academic units; specifically, these offices maintain records, assess evidence, and track submissions for both internal auditing and assessment. Maintaining manual and fragmented processes risks documents for delayed verification and incomplete records. Further, this compromises the visibility of compliance status among institutions and programs alike.  
 Using the Object-Oriented Analysis and Design Methodology (OOADM), KanayoKizito and Nwabueze (2019) proposed a Web-Based Student Record Management System for higher education. Through this methodology, the study focused on identifying system objects and defining their relationships, upon which system components were structured based on user roles and real-world entities. Through this approach the system was allowed to support multiple user roles, such as students, lecturers, parents, administrators, and organizations, each of which has been granted specific access and functions. Hasibuan et al. (2026), on the other hand, focused on building a web-based record management system for the Education Quality Assurance Agency to provide the said agency with an archiving system. Their study utilized the Waterfall approach, along with PHP, MySQL and Bootstrap, to provide control over the incoming and outgoing records, manage and control user accounts, oversee the uploading of records via recapitulation, and provide the ability to produce various records. The prior indicates that enhanced access and accuracy are a result of implementing such web-based applications to render management of records, while the latter study describes improvements in the retrieval, organization and efficiency of and security surrounding quality assurance related documents through such applications.

	Jannah et al․ (2022) stressed the control‚ compliance‚ and monitoring functions that bring the topic closer to internal quality assurance rather than external․ The study employed a descriptive method which consisted of observation and document analysis to study the audit of a Web-based electronic records management system in higher education institutions․ In contrast‚ the above-mentioned study focused on the control practices of accuracy‚ protection‚ conformity‚ and completeness (ACDC) when verifying electronic documents‚ rather than investigating the digital preservation of such documents․ With respect to the above-mentioned focus on control practices‚ Lemosnero et al․ (2026) developed a quality assurance monitoring system for an Academic Standards Compliance and Document Management System (ASCOM)‚ applying the Waterfall model and IEEE software engineering recommendations․ In addition to the study's insistence upon auditing and oversight of electronic records‚ it told how such concerns could be realized in the creation of a system to ensure compliance with academic quality standards․ The study recommended that quality assurance systems be assessed according to their technical performance and user experience․

### **2.1.6 AACCUP Accreditation in Higher Education** {#2.1.6-aaccup-accreditation-in-higher-education}

The Accrediting Agency of Chartered Colleges and Universities in the Philippines (AACCUP) plays an important role in maintaining the quality of State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) in the country. De Lara (2017) expressed the need to develop a common Outcomes-Based Quality Assurance (OBQA) accrediting tool with the standards of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) to improve quality assurance procedures in higher education institutions. The instrument has 10 categories of accreditation, namely, Vision, Mission, Goals and Objectives (VMGO), Faculty, Curriculum and Instruction, Support to Students, Research, Extension and Community Involvement, Library, Physical Plant and Facilities, Laboratories, and Administration.

The report also emphasised the role of AACCUP accreditation in assisting higher education institutions in implementing outcomes-based education (OBE) and in promoting continuous quality improvement. Quality assurance techniques can help institutions align academic programmes, services and institutional procedures more closely with national standards and expected learning outcomes.

The use of OBE in higher education institutions was explored by Hapinat (2023) using the most popular accrediting criteria for quality assurance evaluation. VMGO, Faculty, Curriculum and Instruction, and Support to Students were rated “very satisfactory” reflecting high degree of compliance with the criteria and quality assurance requirements of the accrediting body. 

The investigations proved that AACCUP accreditation involves systematic document organisation, monitoring, compliance, and evidence management across many certification domains. This reveals the need for a central system to assist higher education institutions with document accessibility, quality assurance and monitoring.

## **2.2 Synthesis** {#2.2-synthesis}

Universities and institutions are increasingly adopting web-based document management and monitoring systems to make handling records and accreditation documents more efficient, accessible, and secure. A central repository, monitoring tools and digital workflows can significantly reduce the volume of manual effort that needs to be completed, helping with better document management practices as well as record-keeping. In the study by Hermosa et al․ (2023)‚ Nagrama et al․ (2024)‚ and Dres and Rabut (2025)‚ both retrieving and tracking the storage of objects improved the organization of tasks․

The reviewed studies indicated that monitoring systems that allowed them to comply with these requirements were an essential factor contributing to the operation of quality assurance activities in educational institutions․ Kommey et al․ (2022) and Lemosnero et al. (2026) ‚ the monitoring systems used by institutions to track compliance records also helped improve inter-office coordination․ In addition‚ it also mandates role-based access control and security mechanisms for the protection of confidential institutional records by granting rights to authorized users․

The institutional accreditation study of the Accrediting Agency of Chartered Colleges and Universities in the Philippines (AACCUP) resorted to document management‚ monitoring and quality assurance‚ but De Lara (2017) and Hapinat (2023) also aptly noted that many an accreditation area is not efficient in terms of systematically addressing the institutional data and monitoring or verifying the compliance․

In the field of Optical Character Recognition (OCR)‚ research has shown that OCR technology can convert scanned documents into editable digital text and‚ when paired with image pre-processing techniques‚ improve the efficiency of digitizing documents and reduce the need for manual text encoding (Pham et al․ 2022‚ Zain et al․ 2025)․ However, the studies also highlighted the need for user validation to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the extracted information before storing records into the system.

Currently, the accreditation documents, monitoring records, and document requests of Bicol University’s Internal Quality Assurance Office are managed through manual and fragmented processes. During the development of IQArchive, the researchers considered the findings of the reviewed literature and studies. The proposed system provides a single web-based platform for centralised document management, accreditation monitoring, OCR-assisted document encoding, notifications and role-based access control to improve document accessibility, monitoring efficiency and overall quality assurance operations within the university.

## **2.3 Gap Bridged by the Study** {#2.3-gap-bridged-by-the-study}

Research has shown that document tracking, storage, retrieval and digitising can be improved by web-based document management systems, document monitoring tools and OCR technologies. However, it was revealed in the literature analysed that such components are usually implemented separately. OCR applications are mainly limited to archive processing and scanned document digitisation rather than accreditation monitoring workflows, but most of the accreditation related systems are based on centralised storage, monitoring or access control.

The synthesis also found limited integration of OCR-assisted encoding with certification document management and monitoring systems. Previous research has not put much emphasis on the integration of a single platform for internal quality assurance procedures such as a centralised document repository, role-based access, notifications, accreditation monitoring and OCR-assisted processing.

With this need IQArchive provides a single web-based solution with role-based access control, document encoding with OCR assistance, notifications, document management and accreditation monitoring. This holistic plan will improve the Internal Quality Assurance Office of Bicol University in terms of document accessibility, monitoring effectiveness and compliance tracking.

## **2.4 Concept of the Study** {#2.4-concept-of-the-study}

### **2.4.1 Theoretical Framework** {#2.4.1-theoretical-framework}

Several theories serve as guiding principles for the design, assessment of the system, and user adoption for IQArchive system development and assessment.

In this study, the development framework focuses primarily on the Rapid Application Development (RAD) Model, first presented by James Martin in 1991\. RAD is defined by fast, user-involved development cycles, rapid refinement, and user-prototype feedback. Technical expertise on the end user’s part is the primary concern by which the RAD model became a prudent choice for the development of IQArchive. Unlike more traditional models of development in which systematic requirements are specified prior to development, the RAD methodology empowers the researchers to develop a working prototype after each of the iterations, to which the client reacts and subsequently provides feedback. This inherently user-centered model helps diminish the distance between the needs of the user and the final product, as well as any misalignment between the final product and the office workflow.

The DeLone and McLean Information Systems Success Model (2003) also assists in the development process and the completed system’s evaluation. To the extent of this model, system and information quality, and net benefits are crucial factors of Information Systems (IS) Success. With regards to IQArchive, this model will assist in evaluating whether the system functions as intended, information and documentation are accurate, and the system provides benefits through decreased manual workload and improved compliance to accreditation monitoring for the IQA Office and its stakeholders.

The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), proposed by Davis (1989), also adds to the study by stating that the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness act as deciding factors in the process of deciding if the system will be adopted. Because the IQA Office is limitedly familiar with document management systems, it is appropriate to utilize the TAM to justify the user interface and features designed to ease the use of the IQArchive system. In this case, user-friendly navigation and document uploading, coupled with the automated and OCR-assisted digitized document management, all serve the purpose of improving usability for the users.

Finally, the evaluation standard by which the IQArchive will undergo assessment is the ISO 25010 Quality Model focusing on core quality characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability. Through this assessment, the model ensures that the system satisfies a recognized international benchmark, in addition to the efficiency and functionality it provides.

### **2.4.2 Conceptual Framework** {#2.4.2-conceptual-framework}

| Input |  | Process |  | Output |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Documents |  | Document upload and storage |  | Controlled copy |
| Document metadata |  | Metadata tagging and classification  |  | Controlled document records |
| Scanned data |  | OCR-assisted text extraction |  | Controlled data |
| Image data |  | Image preprocessing for OCR |  | Validated extracted information |
| User credentials and access roles |  | User authentication and role-based access control |  | Authorized user access |
| Document request details |  | Document request review, approval, or denial |  | Document request status  |
| Accreditation submission details  |  | Accreditation submission monitoring |  | Submission status records |
| Deadlines and schedules  |  | Deadline tracking and notification processing |  | Deadline reminders and missed-deadline alerts |
| Search and retrieval queries |  | Search, filtering, and document retrieval |  | Retrieved authorized documents |
| User feedback and validation input |  | User review and validation of OCR-extracted data |  | Verified accreditation-related data |

**Figure 1\.** Conceptual Framework

Figure 1 presents the Input-Process-Output (IPO) conceptual framework that illustrates the core operational mechanics and data lifecycle of IQArchive. The framework carefully charts how the system accepts specified data, manipulates and maintains that data through its built-in capabilities, and produces the subsequent outputs that meet the document management and accreditation monitoring needs of the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office.

The input column contains raw data, user actions and parameters that are given into the system to commence its functions. These inputs are the document-related resources such raw documents, scanned data, picture data and metadata. It also incorporates user driven factors like credentials, access roles, search and retrieval queries etc. Monitoring variables include document request information, accreditation submission details, deadlines etc. Besides, it considers human-in-the-loop interactions, i.e., user feedback and validation input required to check the retrieved data. These are the various data points the system needs to cater for collectively to enable complete document management. 

The process column describes the automated actions and system core functionalities executed on the corresponding inputs. This stage comprises the several functional modules of the system, starting with data acquisition techniques such as document upload and storage, metadata tagging, picture preprocessing, and OCR-aided text extraction. It also enforces security features through user authentication and role-based access restriction. The system manages workflow by reviewing document requests, tracking accreditation submissions and processing deadline tracking and notifications. Finally, it allows data access and quality control through search, filtering and document retrieval and user inspection and validation of data retrieved through OCR.

The output column describes the resulting data, the records created and the system responses after processing. These outputs are in direct response to the organisational and compliance needs of the IQA Office. The monitoring and retrieval capabilities of the system, on the other hand, generate actionable outputs such as document request statuses, submission status records, deadline reminders, missed-deadline alarms, and successfully retrieved authorised documents. Finally, this structured flow guarantees that the office will have access to confirmed data linked to accreditation at all times. 

## **2.5 Definition of Terms** {#2.5-definition-of-terms}

For better understanding of the idea presented in this study and to better understand the key terms used, the following important terms are defined:

**Accreditation Compliance** This pertains to the degree to which an institution meets the established standards stipulated by an accrediting body, indicating adherence to quality assurance requirements (AACCUP, 2020). In this study, it refers to the colleges and offices of Bicol University submitting the requirements for the submission of documents as required by AACCUP which is monitored through the IQArchive system.

**Authorized Users**  This is the people that are given verified permission to access a system or resource as per the assigned roles and credentials (Stallings, 2018).  In this study it refers to the IQA office staff, administrators, college and programme heads, faculty and university executives who are given role-based access to use IQArchive.

**Centralized Repository**  This refers to a single, unified digital storage system that consolidates all uploaded documents from across an organization, organized and maintained for efficient access and retrieval.  ScienceDirect Topics (n.d.). In this study, it pertains to the consolidated digital storage in IQArchive that has all the documents, policies, memoranda, issuances, and accreditation records of university colleges and offices uploaded.  

**Deadline Notification**  This is a system-generated automatic alert to notify users of approaching or elapsed due dates for required actions or submissions (Turban et al., 2009). In this study, it refers to system-generated alerts sent to authorised users reminding them of upcoming or missed document submission deadlines as defined by the IQA office. 

**Document Management System**  This refers to a computer system for storing, managing, tracking and controlling the movement of electronic documents and images of paper-based information obtained from document scanners (Sprague, 1995\) . In this study, IQArchive pertains to the platform developed for IQA Office of Bicol University for uploading, organising, retrieving and monitoring official documents for the purpose of accreditation compliance.

**Document Monitoring**  This encompasses the systematic process of tracking and supervising the submission status of required documents within an organization (ISO 15489-1, 2016). In this study, it refers to the module within IQArchive that enables the IQA Office to track the submission status of required documents per university program and monitor compliance with accreditation deadlines. 

**Document Retrieval** The process of searching and retrieving of stored documents from within a system using search and filtering features (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.). In this study it refers to the ability of authorised users to find and access stored documents in IQArchive via search keywords, category filters and other tools provided by the system for retrieval. 

**Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office** is an organisational unit responsible for establishing, implementing and monitoring quality standards in academic and administrative operations in a higher education institution (UNESCO, 2007). In this study, the term refers to the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office of Bicol University which is mandated to develop and implement a comprehensive quality assurance system in order to maintain, monitor and enhance the academic standards of the University’s programmes.

**ISO/IEC 25010**  This is a product quality model for ICT and software products consisting of nine characteristics such as functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability for the International Organisation for Standardisation. (ISO 25010, 2023).    In this study, it serves as the evaluation framework used to assess IQArchive in terms of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and security, with IQA staff and IT professionals as respondents. 

**Optical Character Recognition** This refers to a technology that enables converting images of typed/printed text into machine-readable format from scanned documents or photos (ScienceDirect Topics, n.d.). In this study, it refers to the feature in IQArchive that allows IQA office staff to digitize printed or scanned physical documents limited to printed text so that they can be uploaded, stored, and managed within the system. 

**Role Based Access Control**  This is a security mechanism that limits system access based on user roles within an organisation so that users are only allowed to do things that are relevant to their jobs (Ferraiolo et al., 2001). In this study it means the access control system of IQArchive which provides different levels of system permissions to IQA staff, administrators, heads of college and other authorised users based on their roles.

## **3.2 Methods** {#3.2-methods}

	In this section, the proponents present the methodology chosen to be applied in the development of the proposed system. 

### **3.2.1 Needs Assessment** {#3.2.1-needs-assessment}

**![][image1]**  
 **Figure 2\.** Guided interview with IQA Office personnel   
The figure shows the researchers conducting a guided interview and requirements gathering session with the personnel of the Internal Quality Assurance (IQA) Office of Bicol University to identify the office’s existing document management practices and accreditation monitoring processes for the development of IQArchive system.

Before proceeding on the designing and development of the IQArchive, a needs assessment was conducted with the IQA Office of Bicol University. This is to establish a clear and complete understanding of its existing document handling practices and to generally determine what the system would need to address. The assessment was carried out through two successive interviews with IQA personnel. First is an initial unstructured interview that explores the current practices in an open and flexible manner. Then, followed by a validation interview involving the IQA director, two IQA members, and the clerical staff to verify, refine or add on the information gathered.

Through the assessment, it was revealed that the IQA Office currently operates without a unified document management infrastructure. Their documents are primarily stored across a combination of physical folders and cabinets designed for documents storage, an informal Google Drive repository, and spreadsheet-based tracking and monitoring tools. None are designed for formal document lifecycle management. The document requests are handled through email or face-to-face communication. A process which does not have a structured workflow, approval trail, or status visibility for either the document requestor or IQA staff. The monitoring of submission statuses is performed manually, and the absence of any notification mechanism exposes the IQA office to delayed or missed submissions, particularly during accreditation periods. These findings confirmed that a centralized document management and monitoring system was really needed. This needs assessment served as the primary basis for defining the functional requirements of IQArchive. 

### **3.2.2 Data Gathering** {#3.2.2-data-gathering}

The Requirements Planning phase of the Rapid Application Development methodology was then followed to obtain‚ analyze and verify the IQArchive Requirements specification using five tools․ The process started with a non-structured interview of a member of the IQA Office in order to gather as much information as possible on the current document management practices․ To confirm the findings from the preliminary investigation and to collect any missing information‚ a validation sheet was subsequently distributed to the entire IQA Office (namely‚ the Director‚ two IQA members and the clerical staff)․ A guided interview form was then used to extract more detailed functional and operational requirements from the IQA staff members․  The researchers then conducted document analysis by reviewing existing documents, forms, tracking spreadsheets, and other records to further understand how the office’s documentation is currently handled and what specific contents it contains. Finally, the researchers developed high-level interface prototypes for IQA stakeholders’ validation. The detailed discussion of each instrument and its findings is presented in 3.2.3.1 Requirements Planning.

### **3.2.3 Software Development Life Cycle**  {#3.2.3-software-development-life-cycle}

The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a critical framework that governs and regulates the process of software development process, this encompasses planning, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance phases (Pargaonkar, 2023). Specifically, the researchers will utilize Rapid Application Development (RAD), which is a rapid prototyping and was established by James Martin in 1991\.   
![][image2]

**Figure 3\.** Rapid Application Development (Martin, 1991\)  
*Source: https://kissflow.com/application-development/rad/rapid-application-development/*

The researchers will use Rapid Application Development. As shown in Figure 3, Rapid Application Development (RAD) focuses on rapid prototyping, continuous feedback from users and iterative improvement, it enables developers to refine the system based on the user needs (Kissflow, 2026). This methodology is suitable for the development of the targeted system, since the system involves features that may require refinement based on actual office workflows, including document storage, accreditation monitoring, deadline notifications, and OCR-assisted encoding. By using RAD, the researchers will be able to accommodate changes, enhance system functionality, and prioritize user requirements, thereby supporting the timely development of a practical and high-quality system.

###### **3.2.3.1 Why RAD over other SDLC Models** {#3.2.3.1-why-rad-over-other-sdlc-models}

To justify the selection of Rapid Application Development as the methodology for IQArchive, it was evaluated against three other widely recognized SDLC models — Waterfall, Agile (Scrum), and Spiral — across criteria relevant to the nature and constraints of this study. Table 3 presents this comparison.

##### 

**Table 3\.** SDLC Model Comparison Matrix

| Criteria | Waterfall | Agile (Scrum) | V-Model | Spiral | RAD |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Flexibility | Very Low | Very High | Low | Medium- High | High |
| Documentation | Comprehensive | Minimal- Moderate | Comprehensive | Extensive | Moderate |
| Customer Involvement | Initial & End | Continuous | Initial & End | Each Cycle | Continuous |
| Testing | After Coding | Each Sprint | Each Phase (Paired) | Each Cycle | Each Iteration |
| Risk Management | Low | Medium | Medium | Very High | Medium |
| Best Project Size | Small-Medium | Any | Medium-Large | Large | Small- Medium |
| Team Experience Needed | Low-Medium | Medium- High | Medium | High | Low- Medium |
| Delivery Approach | Single Final | Incremental | Single Final | Spiral Increments | Prototype- Driven |
| Capstone Suitability | High (fixed req.) | Very High | High (QA focus) | Medium (complex) | **Very High** |

As shown in Table 3, RAD is particularly well-suited to the development of IQArchive for several reasons. First, RAD supports high flexibility and continuous user involvement throughout the development process. These are essential for a system developed in direct coordination with the IQA Office, whose document handling workflows and accreditation monitoring needs ongoing clarification and refinement rather than full upfront specification. Second, RAD's prototype-driven approach will allow the researchers to present working versions per system module to actual users at each iteration, allowing feedback to be given before subsequent development cycles. Third, RAD's team experience requirement and project size suitability aligns well with the constraints of an undergraduate capstone project, where development will occur alongside academic coursework, as well as the client access limited to scheduled consultations. Making RAD more practical than models that demand sustained team ceremonies or formal risk management cycles. In conclusion, the said characteristics make RAD the most appropriate methodology for developing a user-aligned system within the scope and timeline of this study. 

###### **3.2.3.2 Requirements Planning** {#3.2.3.2-requirements-planning}

During the requirements planning phase, the researchers conducted a series of requirements elicitation activities to develop a clear and accurate understanding of the existing workflow of the Internal Quality Assurance Office. The process began with an unstructured interview facilitated by an IQA member. This initial discussion served as the researchers’ entry point into the actual operations of the office, as it introduced them to how accreditation-related documents are received, stored, requested, monitored, and retrieved. The IQA member was able to freely explain the general flow of work in the office, including the use of printed folders, Google Drive storage, spreadsheet-based tracking, and face-to-face or email-based communication. Through this activity, the researchers were able to identify the initial problems encountered by the office and form a preliminary understanding of the possible system features needed for IQArchive.

After the initial interview, the researchers prepared survey-based instruments to verify and deepen the information they had gathered. This second elicitation activity involved the whole IQA Office, including the Director of IQA, two IQA members, and the clerical staff. The first instrument used was a preliminary validation sheet, which contained statements reflecting the researchers’ current understanding of the IQA Office. Through this instrument, the respondents were able to confirm which statements were accurate, identify partially accurate or inaccurate information, and provide corrections or additional details. The validation sheet covered the office’s main functions, documents handled, accreditation monitoring practices, current document storage and workflow, users and access control, and reporting practices. This allowed the researchers to correct possible assumptions from the first interview and ensure that the identified requirements were grounded on the actual practices of the IQA Office.

This interview form was designed to help the researchers gather further details in addition to the existing knowledge, as compared to the preliminary validation sheet that focused on confirming the said knowledge.  The form contained questions targeting document management needs, accreditation monitoring, report generation, security and access control, OCR-related considerations, and general system expectations in particular. The instrument helped the researchers clarify the required features of IQArchive, including the centralized document repository, document request workflow, monitoring module, report generation, deadline notification, role-based access control, and OCR-assisted upload feature.

Following, the researchers performed document analysis to support the information gathered from the interviews and survey instruments. As given permission by the IQA, the researchers examined the existing documents, forms, records, and tracking files, which helped them understand and specify the actual data handled by the office, as well as how they are handled.

This activity helped the researchers identify the document categories, accreditation-related information, submission status data, and monitoring records that needed to be represented in the proposed system. Through document analysis, the researchers were able to connect the verbal explanations of the IQA personnel with the actual documents and records used in their daily operations.

Lastly, the researchers used prototyping to validate the proposed direction of the system with the intended users. Initial interface layouts and feature representations were presented to show how the document repository, document request workflow, monitoring dashboard, notification features, and OCR-assisted upload process would function. The feedback gathered from this activity helped the researchers refine the planned modules before proceeding to actual system development. Through these elicitation techniques, the researchers were able to establish a more complete basis for designing the system architecture, database structure, user interface, and major system modules of IQArchive.

## **3.2.3.2.1 Use Case Diagram**

**Figure 4\.** IQArchive Use Case Diagram  
The diagram defines five actors: System Administrator, IQA Staff, College/Department Head and Program Chair, Faculty Member, and University Administrator/Executive. These actors interact with the system through seven functional modules contained within the system boundary: Authentication, Document Repository, Document Request Workflow, Accreditation Monitoring, Report Generation, OCR-Assisted Upload, and User Management.  
The Authentication module has been implemented‚ which allows all five actors to log in‚ log out and manage their own account․ It is a secure entry point where the remaining modules are accessed according to the assigned actor roles․ In the Document Repository module‚ IQA Staff can upload‚ classify‚ update‚ archive‚ limit access‚ retrieve and search for documents․ College/Department Head and Program Chair can upload‚ retrieve and search documents․ Faculty Members and University Administrators/Executives can only retrieve and search documents․ The Document Request Workflow module allows College/Department Heads‚ Program Chair and Faculty Members to submit document requests and view the status of requests․ IQA Staff can view‚ approve‚ or deny the requests․ Each of the two «include» relationships in the Use Case diagram‚ Approve Document Request and Deny Document Request‚ includes View Document Request‚ because IQA Staff members can view requests before they can approve or deny those requests․  
Within Accreditation Monitoring‚ IQA Staff can set accreditation deadlines and cycles‚ view submission statuses‚ view the monitoring dashboard‚ and receive deadline notifications․ The College/Department Head and Program Chair can view submission statuses for their units and receive deadline notifications․ University Administrator/Executive has read-only access to the monitoring dashboard․ An "extend" relationship is defined from Receive Deadline Notification to View Monitoring Dashboard․ The user may optionally navigate to the View Monitoring Dashboard when a Notification is received․ In the Report Generation module, IQA Staff can generate and view compliance reports, while University Administrator/Executive can only view them. The OCR-Assisted Upload module is accessible exclusively to IQA Staff and models a sequential chain of «include» relationships: Upload Scanned Document includes Review OCR-Extracted Text, which in turn includes Confirm and Save Extracted Data, as each step is always required before the next can proceed. Finally, the User Management module is restricted to the System Administrator, who can create user accounts, assign roles, deactivate accounts, and view the system audit log.

###### **3.2.3.3 User Design** {#3.2.3.3-user-design}

The second phase of the RAD model is user design. In this phase, the researchers translated the gathered requirements into visual and functional representations of the proposed system. The design process will focus on creating a user-friendly and efficient interface that would allow authorized users to do the specific functions with minimal difficulty.

The researchers will prepare system design materials such as interface layouts, navigation flow, database design, and module structures. Figma will be used in designing the UI/UX of IQArchive. The design will focus on simplicity and ease of navigation to ensure that IQA staff and other authorized users could operate the system without any difficulty. The main modules considered in the design include user management, document repository, document categorization, search and retrieval, accreditation monitoring, deadline notification, and OCR-assisted encoding.

In this phase, the researchers also considered the feedback and expected workflow of the IQA Office. Since the system is intended to support accreditation-related document management, the design was structured to reflect how documents are categorized, submitted, reviewed, monitored, and retrieved. The user design phase will allow the researchers to refine the proposed system before actual development, ensuring that the planned features are aligned with the needs of the target users.

## **3.3 OCR Integration Approach** {#3.3-ocr-integration-approach}

This section describes the technical approach, the OCR engine selected, the preprocessing measures applied, and the validation procedure required before extracted text is saved into the monitoring system.

### **3.3.1 OCR Engine** {#3.3.1-ocr-engine}

The system will use Tesseract OCR, an open-source optical character recognition engine maintained by Google, as the primary text extraction tool. Tesseract was selected for several reasons. First, it supports PHP integration through available wrapper libraries, making it compatible with the Laravel-based backend of IQArchive. Second, it is capable of processing standard printed document formats, including typed memos, accreditation result forms, and compliance records which are the document types that are most commonly submitted to the IQA Office in physical or scanned form. Third, as an open-source tool, it does not introduce licensing costs or third-party service dependencies, which is appropriate for a system intended for institutional deployment within a state university.

Tesseract performs best on clearly printed, properly oriented documents. OCR accuracy may be reduced by low-resolution scans, skewed or rotated pages, stained or degraded paper, and complex multi-column or tabular layouts. These limitations are consistent with findings reported in the related literature, where preprocessing was shown to significantly improve OCR output for scanned institutional documents (Pham et al., 2022).

### **3.3.2 User Review and Validation** {#3.3.2-user-review-and-validation}

Because OCR output is not guaranteed to be perfectly accurate, the system adopts an assisted encoding model rather than an automatic population model. After the OCR engine extracts text from an uploaded document, the extracted content is displayed to the authorized user in an editable review interface alongside the original uploaded image. The user is required to review, correct, and confirm the extracted information before it is saved into the monitoring module as an accreditation record.

This user-in-the-loop approach serves two purposes. First, it ensures that inaccurate or incomplete OCR output does not propagate unchecked into the system's accreditation compliance records. Second, it preserves accountability, as the authorized user who reviews and confirms the data takes ownership of the saved record. The OCR feature is therefore positioned as a productivity aid — reducing the effort of encoding by providing a pre-filled draft — rather than as a fully automated data entry mechanism. This framing is consistent with how similar OCR-assisted systems in institutional contexts have been designed, where human verification remains a required step before extracted data is committed to the database (Zain et al., 2025).

## **3.4 Evaluation Procedure** {#3.4-evaluation-procedure}

The developed system will be evaluated against the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model focusing on Functional Suitability‚ Performance Efficiency‚ Compatibility‚ Usability‚ Reliability‚ Security‚ Maintainability‚ and Portability․ These quality characteristics were chosen to evaluate the quality of the developed software product because these are most closely aligned with IQArchive's role as a document management and monitoring system for the Internal Quality Assurance Office of Bicol University․ 

### **3.4.1 Pilot Testing** {#3.4.1-pilot-testing}

Before the formal evaluation‚ a pilot test with 2-3 users from the target population of system users (IQA staff or IT-literate staff with experience in document management and retrieval) will take place․ The pilot test will focus on a walkthrough of the core functionality of IQArchive: document upload and retrieval‚ document request workflow‚ and document tracking and notification functionality․ During the walkthrough‚ typical tasks that users would perform should be carried out‚ in order to identify usability problems‚ inconsistencies in the look and feel and navigation of the interface‚ and any missing functionality that was not apparent during the development of the system․ In addition‚ the evaluation questionnaire should be reviewed and answered by the participants to enable the evaluation team to assess the item clarity‚ appropriateness‚ and completeness․ The results of the pilot test will be used to make any final modifications to the system and the evaluation instrument prior to the actual evaluation․ 

### **3.4.2 ISO/IEC 25010** {#3.4.2-iso/iec-25010}

**Respondents.** The evaluation will involve a target of approximately 10 to 15 respondents drawn from two groups. The first group consists of IQA office staff, including personnel directly involved in document management, accreditation monitoring, and system use. The second group consists of IT professionals who can evaluate the system's technical qualities, as well as other intended users of the system — specifically, college and department heads, program chairs, faculty members, and university administrators whose roles involve accreditation-related activities or document access within the IQA's operational scope. 

**Sampling Methodology.** Respondents will be selected through total population sampling. All available IQA office staff will be included, as the office operates with a defined and limited number of personnel directly involved in accreditation and document management. IT professionals and other intended users will be identified and included based on their institutional role and direct relevance to the system's functions. No random selection will be applied; every individual who falls within the defined respondent groups and is available for the evaluation will be included. 

**Data Collection Instrument.** The system will be evaluated using a structured survey questionnaire developed in accordance with the ISO/IEC 25010 quality criteria identified for this study. The questionnaire will be organized into sections corresponding to each quality characteristic and will use a five-point Likert scale to measure the level of agreement of each respondent regarding the quality and performance of the system, as presented in Table 4\. 

**Evaluation Process.** The evaluation will be conducted by first presenting and demonstrating IQArchive to the respondents, allowing them to navigate and interact with its major features — including document uploading and retrieval, the document request workflow, the monitoring module, deadline notifications, and the OCR-assisted upload feature. After the demonstration and hands-on use, respondents will be asked to accomplish the evaluation questionnaire. The computed mean values will be interpreted against the Likert scale in Table 4 to determine respondents' level of agreement with each evaluation criterion. The findings will be used to assess the overall acceptability and quality of IQArchive and to identify areas for further improvement.

##### **Table 4\.** Likert Scale

| Range | Meaning | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 5 | Strongly Agree | The system has functional completeness of tasks, is effective and reliable. |
| 4 | Agree | The system has somehow functional completeness of tasks, is somehow effective and reliable. |
| 3 | Neutral | The system has slightly functional completeness of tasks, is slightly effective and reliable. |
| 2 | Disagree | The system has slightly no functional completeness of tasks, is slightly not effective and reliable. |
| 1 | Strongly Disagree | The system has no functional completeness of tasks, is not effective and reliable. |

## **3․5 Security Architecture** {#3․5-security-architecture}

Since all of the data processed and stored by IQArchive is highly sensitive‚ including university confidential information‚ accreditation information‚ and user information‚ security is a high priority for the IQArchive architecture and implementation․ This section will discuss the IQArchive security model‚ role based security‚ data encryption‚ classification of confidential data‚ and privacy compliance․

### **3․5․1 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** {#3․5․1-role-based-access-control-(rbac)}

IQArchive implements RBAC (Role-based access control) to grant authorized users access to relevant system functionalities and data based on their role within the institution and the role's prerogatives with respect to the system․ The information contained within the system is not accessible to any one user group․ Once an user is authenticated‚ the system grants access to information based on the user's assigned role․ The system has the following user roles and accesses:

**System Administrator** — the account type with full administrative rights to the system․ This user creates and manages user accounts‚ assigns roles to users‚ configures the system‚ and views audit logs․ The System Administrator is not a participant in document workflows as a regular user and does not have discretionary authority to approve or deny document requests on behalf of IQA staff․

**College / Department Head and Program Chair** — has access to documents and monitoring reports for the college‚ department‚ or academic program under his or her direction․ They can upload requested documents‚ request documents that the unit has uploaded‚ view the status of submitted documents‚ and view and be notified of upcoming compliance deadlines․ They may not inspect documents or monitoring records of other colleges‚ departments‚ or programs․

**Faculty Member** — has access to any documents provided by IQA staff or the faculty member's college or department head‚ can submit document requests‚ and can view notifications of requests submitted for their unit․ They cannot access the monitoring module or accreditation compliance records․

**University Administrator / Executive** — has read-only access to system-wide reports and dashboards‚ used to monitor summaries and compliance activities

### **3.5.2 Data Encryption** {#3.5.2-data-encryption}

IQArchive encrypts all sensitive data both at rest and in transit․ All data in the system database is encrypted with the Advanced Encryption Standard 256 bit (AES-256) algorithm․ AES-256 is the minimum standard for encryption‚ and is considered international best practice for securing institutional data that is sensitive or confidential․

All communication between the client and server is encrypted with HTTPS and TLS protocols to prevent eavesdropping and tampering․ The server doesn't store the user's password in plain text‚ but rather it hashes it with a strong cryptographically secure hashing algorithm․ Session tokens are created during login and destroyed during logout or when the user session expires․

### **3.5.3 Data Privacy Compliance** {#3.5.3-data-privacy-compliance}

IQArchive is compliant with Republic Act No․ 10173‚ otherwise known as the Data Privacy Act of 2012 of the Philippines‚ and the Implementing Rules and Regulations․ Pursuant to RA 10173‚ the system only processes personal data to attain its institutional purpose‚ which is to ease and process documents and monitor compliance requirements in the IQA Office of the Bicol University․

Data privacy notices are posted in all forms in the system requiring personal data of the system user‚ such as the user registration form‚ document request submission form‚ or any other form requiring the entry of individual or institutional data in the system by the user․ The data privacy notice informs the user of the purpose/s of the collection of personal data‚ the legal basis of processing‚ the individuals or entities to whom the data shall be disclosed‚ and the rights considered under the Data Privacy Act (such as data access‚ data correction‚ and data erasure/deletion)․

IQArchive will collect‚ store‚ and process user personal data for institutional purposes to the extent necessary for the performance of authorized functions of Bicol University․ It will not disclose the personal data to any entity except those authorized by Bicol University or to any user except those under Section 3․5․1 of this policy․
